opus-5.5.text:
I think about hallucination as a symptom of how these models are trained rather than a bug you can patch in one place. A language model is fundamentally learning to predict the next token, so it's very good at producing text that is fluent and plausible. But plausible isn't the same as grounded. When the model doesn't have strong evidence for something, either because the fact was rare in the training data or because the question pushes it outside what it has seen, it still produces a confident-sounding continuation. That's essentially what we call a hallucination.

It helps me to separate it into a few buckets. One is factual hallucination: the model states something about the world that's just wrong, like a citation that doesn't exist or a date that's off. Another is faithfulness to context: you give the model a document and ask it to summarize, and it introduces details that weren't in the source. And then there's reasoning errors, where each step looks locally reasonable but the chain drifts somewhere incorrect. Those have somewhat different causes and different mitigations.

Scale does help to a degree. As we trained larger models, we saw them memorize more facts and become better calibrated on things they had seen often. But scale alone doesn't solve the long tail. So a lot of the interesting work is around grounding, retrieving relevant information and conditioning the model on it, and around getting the model to know what it doesn't know: calibration, expressing uncertainty, being willing to abstain. Techniques like chain-of-thought can also help with reasoning-type errors, because you make the intermediate steps explicit and can check them.

I'd also say that hallucination isn't always bad. In creative writing or brainstorming, that same generative ability is exactly what you want. The real challenge is making the model aware of which mode it's in, so it's imaginative when you ask for imagination and precise and grounded when you ask for facts. That kind of controllability, plus good evaluation of factuality, is where I think a lot of the progress needs to happen.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and I think the first thing I'd say is that hallucination isn't really a bug in the model so much as a consequence of what we trained it to do. A language model is fundamentally trained to predict the next token given the context. We never asked it to be truthful. We asked it to produce text that looks like the text it's seen. So when it generates a citation that doesn't exist, or a date that's slightly off, it's doing exactly what the objective rewards: producing something fluent and plausible. The model doesn't have a notion of "I don't know this" built into the pretraining objective.

When we were working on PaLM, this was something we saw pretty clearly. The model got dramatically better at reasoning tasks, at few-shot learning, at things like explaining jokes, as we scaled up. But scale alone doesn't fix hallucination in the same way. In some sense, a larger model can hallucinate more convincingly, because its outputs are more fluent and more confident-sounding. The errors become harder to catch, not easier.

So I tend to break the problem into a few pieces. One is factual knowledge: does the model actually have the information in its parameters, and is it retrieving it correctly? There's a lot of knowledge compressed into the weights, but it's lossy, and the model will happily interpolate across the gaps. A second piece is calibration: does the model know what it doesn't know? That's where things like asking the model to express uncertainty, or training it with human feedback to say "I'm not sure," come in. And a third piece is grounding. If you give the model access to a retrieval system, or tools, or a document in context, you're shifting the burden from "recall this from memory" to "read this and reason about it," which models are much better at.

I'll also say the word "hallucination" gets used for a lot of different things. Sometimes it's the model confabulating a fact. Sometimes it's the model being internally inconsistent across a long chain of reasoning. Sometimes it's just following the user's framing even when the premise is wrong. Those probably need different fixes. Chain-of-thought prompting, for example, helps a lot with the reasoning consistency piece, because the model is externalizing intermediate steps that we can inspect. It does much less for the model simply not knowing something.

The honest answer is I don't think we fully solve hallucination with the current paradigm. What we can do is reduce it, make it detectable, and design systems where the model isn't the sole source of truth. For a lot of applications, that's enough. For others, like medical or legal settings, you really want the model grounded in verifiable sources with a human in the loop. I think the interesting research direction is getting models to be more faithful to their evidence and more honest about uncertainty, rather than just more fluent.

astra-6.text:
I think of hallucination as a model generating something that sounds plausible but isn’t grounded in facts or in the information you’ve provided. A language model is trained to predict text, and producing a likely continuation is not necessarily the same as producing a truthful answer.

The context matters, too. If you’re asking the model to write a creative story, inventing details may be exactly what you want. If you’re asking it a factual question, that same behavior becomes a problem. So we need to think about how to ground its answers in evidence, how to evaluate whether that evidence supports what it says, and how to get it to acknowledge when it doesn’t know.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about hallucination as the model generating something that sounds plausible but isn’t grounded in facts. The model is trained to predict the next token, and that objective doesn’t, by itself, guarantee that what it says is true. So you can get a very fluent, very confident answer that’s incorrect.

An important question is what we expect from the application. In a creative task, generating something new can be useful. If you’re asking a factual question, you want the answer grounded in reliable information, and you want the model to recognize when it doesn’t have enough information to answer. That’s where grounding, evaluation, and expressing uncertainty become important. I think of this as a system-level challenge as well as a model-training challenge.
